passages.original: Quod si exsecrarentur, mutarent sententiam, et unum Deum quærerent I, qucm solum supra mentes nostras esse, ei a quo omnem animam ct lotum istum mundum fabricatum esse constaret. Postea suavius ad legendum, quam potentius ad persuadendum scripsit Plato. Non euim sic isti nati erant, ut populorum suorum opinionem ad verum cultum ,'cti Dei, a simulacrorum superstitione atque ab hujus mundi vanilale converterent. Itaque et ipse Socrates cum populo simulacra venerabatur, et post ejus damnationem mortemque, nemo ausus est jurare per canem, nee appellare quem.
passages.english: But if they had abhorred these things, they would have changed their opinion and sought the one God, whom alone it was established to be above our minds, [and] by whom every soul and this whole world had been fashioned. Afterwards Plato wrote more agreeably for reading than powerfully for persuading. For these men had not been born such that they could turn the opinion of their peoples from the superstition of images and from the vanity of this world to the true worship of the true God. passages.notes: The first sentence is grammatically awkward: 'ei a quo' appears corrupt (perhaps for 'et a quo'), and is translated as 'by whom'. 'quærerent I' has a stray mark, omitted. ',cti Dei' is read as 'veri Dei' ('the true God'). The passage breaks off mid-sentence. The context after shows it continues 'any stone Jupiter'; Socrates' oath 'by the dog' is alluded to.

passages.original: Quid jam de anima ipsa dicam vegetante modulum corporis sui, quomodo eum numerose moveat, quomodo appetat convenientia, quomodo vincat aut cavent obsistentia quantum potest, et ad unum sensum incolumitatis referens omnia, unitatem illam conditricem naturarum omnium, multo evidentius quam corpus insinuet ? lequor de vermicu!o animante qualicumque. Cineris et stercoris laudem verissime atque uberrime plerique dixerunt (Cato apud Ciceronem, in Catone majore). Quid ergo mirum cst, si hominis animam, quae ubicumque sit et qualiscumque sit, omni corpore est melior, dicam pulchre ordinari , et de pcenis ejus alias pulchritudines fleri, cum ibi non sit quando misera est, ubi beatos esse decet, sed ibi sit ubi esse miseros decet?
passages.english: What now shall I say of the soul itself, which animates the small measure of its body: how it moves it rhythmically, how it seeks what suits it, how it overcomes or guards against what opposes it as far as it can, and, referring everything to the one sense of its own safety, suggests far more evidently than the body that unity which is the founder of all natures? I am speaking of any living little worm whatever. Very many have spoken most truly and most fully in praise of ashes and dung (Cato in Cicero, in the Cato Maior). What wonder is it, then, if I say that the soul of a human being, which, wherever it is and of whatever kind it is, is better than every body, is beautifully ordered, and that from its punishments other beauties come about, since, when it is wretched, it is not where it is fitting for the blessed to be, but is where it is fitting for the wretched to be?
passages.notes: Scanning errors read as intended: 'cavent' as 'caveat', 'lequor' as 'loquor', 'fleri' as 'fieri', 'pcenis' as 'poenis'. The parenthetical reference to Cato is an editorial citation in the printed text.
